claim: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) respond when an animal occupies a periodic lattice of 'grid fields' in the environment.
source: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) respond when an animal occupies a periodic lattice of 'grid fields' in the environment.
evidence: This is a well-established finding cited in the introduction, supported by reference to Hafting et al., 2005.

claim: The grids are organized in modules with spatial periods, or scales, clustered around discrete values separated on average by ratios in the range 1.4–1.7.
source: The grids are organized in modules with spatial periods, or scales, clustered around discrete values separated on average by ratios in the range 1.4–1.7.
evidence: This statement summarizes experimental observations about grid module organization.

claim: In attractor network models of grid formation, the grid scale of a single module is set by the distance of recurrent inhibition between neurons.
source: In attractor network models of grid formation, the grid scale of a single module is set by the distance of recurrent inhibition between neurons.
evidence: This describes a known property of continuous attractor models.

claim: The MEC forms a hierarchy of discrete modules if a smooth increase in inhibition distance along its dorso-ventral axis is accompanied by excitatory interactions along this axis.
source: We show that the MEC forms a hierarchy of discrete modules if a smooth increase in inhibition distance along its dorso-ventral axis is accompanied by excitatory interactions along this axis.
evidence: This is the main theoretical prediction of the model, supported by simulations shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Constant scale ratios between successive modules arise through geometric relationships between triangular grids and have values that fall within the observed range.
source: Moreover, constant scale ratios between successive modules arise through geometric relationships between triangular grids and have values that fall within the observed range.
evidence: This claim is supported by the commensurate lattice analysis in Figure 5 and the scale ratio measurements in Figure 3C.

claim: Grid cells have a spatially modulated firing rate that peaks when an animal reaches certain locations in its environment (Hafting et al., 2005).
source: A grid cell has a spatially modulated firing rate that peaks when an animal reaches certain locations in its environment (Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a direct citation of an experimental finding.

claim: These locations of high activity form a regular triangular grid with a particular length scale and orientation in space.
source: These locations of high activity form a regular triangular grid with a particular length scale and orientation in space.
evidence: This describes the spatial structure of grid cell firing fields, a well-established experimental observation.

claim: Every animal has many grid cells that collectively span a wide range of scales, with smaller scales enriched dorsally and larger scales ventrally along the longitudinal axis of the MEC (Stensola et al., 2012).
source: Every animal has many grid cells that collectively span a wide range of scales, with smaller scales enriched dorsally and larger scales ventrally along the longitudinal axis of the MEC (Stensola et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct citation of experimental findings about the spatial organization of grid scales.

claim: Grid scales cluster around particular values and thus grid cells are partitioned into modules (Stensola et al., 2012).
source: Instead of being smoothly distributed, grid scales cluster around particular values and thus grid cells are partitioned into modules (Stensola et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct citation of the experimental discovery of grid modules.

claim: Consecutive pairs of modules have scale ratios in the range 1.2–2.0 (Stensola et al., 2012; Barry et al., 2007; Krupic et al., 2015).
source: Consecutive pairs of modules have scale ratios in the range 1.2–2.0 (Stensola et al., 2012; Barry et al., 2007; Krupic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct citation of experimental measurements of scale ratios.

claim: The scale ratio averaged across animals is constant from one pair of modules to the next and lies in the interval 1.4 (Stensola et al., 2012) to 1.7 (Barry et al., 2007; Krupic et al., 2015).
source: The scale ratio averaged across animals is constant from one pair of modules to the next and lies in the interval 1.4 (Stensola et al., 2012) to 1.7 (Barry et al., 2007; Krupic et al., 2015), suggesting that the grid system favors a universal scale ratio in this range.
evidence: This is a direct citation of experimental findings about the constancy of scale ratios.

claim: Encoding spatial information through grid cells with constant scale ratios is thought to provide animals with an efficient way of representing their position within an environment (Moser et al., 2008; Fiete et al., 2008; Mathis et al., 2012; Wei et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015; Sanzeni et al., 2016; Mosheiff et al., 2017).
source: Encoding spatial information through grid cells with constant scale ratios is thought to provide animals with an efficient way of representing their position within an environment (Moser et al., 2008; Fiete et al., 2008; Mathis et al., 2012; Wei et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015; Sanzeni et al., 2016; Mosheiff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct citation of theoretical work on the computational advantages of grid cells.

claim: Periodic representations of space permit a novel mechanism for precise error correction against neural noise (Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011).
source: Moreover, periodic representations of space permit a novel mechanism for precise error correction against neural noise (Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011) and are learned by machines seeking to navigate open environments (Cueva and Wei, 2018; Banino et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct citation of theoretical work on error correction in grid cells.

claim: Periodic representations of space are learned by machines seeking to navigate open environments (Cueva and Wei, 2018; Banino et al., 2018).
source: Moreover, periodic representations of space permit a novel mechanism for precise error correction against neural noise (Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011) and are learned by machines seeking to navigate open environments (Cueva and Wei, 2018; Banino et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct citation of machine learning studies that discovered grid-like representations.

claim: Continuous attractor networks (Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Burak and Fiete, 2009) would currently require discrete changes in scales to be directly imposed as sharp changes in parameters.
source: Continuous attractor networks (Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Burak and Fiete, 2009), a leading model for producing grid cells, would currently require discrete changes in scales to be directly imposed as sharp changes in parameters, as would the oscillatory interference model (Burgess et al., 2007; Hasselmo et al., 2007) or hybrid models (Bush and Burgess, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of existing models based on their structure.

claim: Many sensory and behavioral systems have smooth tuning distributions, such as preferred orientation in visual cortex (Issa et al., 2008) and preferred head direction in the MEC (Taube et al., 1990).
source: In contrast, many sensory and behavioral systems have smooth tuning distributions, such as preferred orientation in visual cortex (Issa et al., 2008) and preferred head direction in the MEC (Taube et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a direct citation of experimental findings about tuning distributions in neural systems.

claim: A self-organizing map model with stripe cell inputs (Grossberg and Pilly, 2012) and a firing rate adaptation model with place cell inputs (Urdapilleta et al., 2017) can generate discrete grid scales, but their ratios are not constant or constant-on-average unless explicitly tuned.
source: A self-organizing map model with stripe cell inputs (Grossberg and Pilly, 2012) and a firing rate adaptation model with place cell inputs (Urdapilleta et al., 2017) can generate discrete grid scales, but their ratios are not constant or constant-on-average unless explicitly tuned.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of existing models based on their published properties.

claim: The inhibition gradient drives an increase in grid scale along the MEC axis.
source: The inhibition gradient drives an increase in grid scale along the MEC axis.
evidence: This is a mechanistic claim supported by the model simulations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The excitatory coupling discourages changes in grid scale and orientation unless they occur through geometric relationships with defined scale ratios and orientation differences.
source: Meanwhile, the excitatory coupling discourages changes in grid scale and orientation unless they occur through geometric relationships with defined scale ratios and orientation differences.
evidence: This is a mechanistic claim supported by the comparison between coupled and uncoupled models in Figure 3 and the lattice analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Competition between the effects of longitudinal excitation and lateral inhibition self-organizes the complete network into a discrete hierarchy of modules.
source: Competition between the effects of longitudinal excitation and lateral inhibition self-organizes the complete network into a discrete hierarchy of modules.
evidence: This is the central mechanistic claim of the paper, supported by simulations in Figures 2-7.

claim: Certain grid relationships are geometrically stable, which makes them, and their associated scale ratios, insensitive to perturbations.
source: Certain grid relationships are geometrically stable, which makes them, and their associated scale ratios, insensitive to perturbations.
evidence: This is supported by the robustness analysis in Figure 4 and the phase diagrams in Figure 5.

claim: The precise ratios that appear depend on the balance between excitation and inhibition and how it varies along the MEC axis.
source: The precise ratios that appear depend on the balance between excitation and inhibition and how it varies along the MEC axis.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter exploration in Figure 5 showing different lattice relationships for different parameter values.

claim: Sampling across a range of these parameters leads to a distribution of scale ratios that matches experiment and is, on average, constant from the smallest to the largest pair of modules.
source: We show that sampling across a range of these parameters leads to a distribution of scale ratios that matches experiment and is, on average, constant from the smallest to the largest pair of modules.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis in Figure 7C,D showing constant-on-average scale ratios.

claim: Networks z = 1, 2, ..., 12 are assembled along the longitudinal MEC axis from dorsal to ventral.
source: We assemble a series of networks along the longitudinal MEC axis, numbering them z = 1, 2, ..., 12 from dorsal to ventral (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the model architecture shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Each network contains the standard 2D continuous attractor architecture of the Burak-Fiete model (Burak and Fiete, 2009).
source: Each network contains the standard 2D continuous attractor architecture of the Burak-Fiete model (Burak and Fiete, 2009).
evidence: This describes the model architecture based on an established model.

claim: Neurons are arranged in a 2D sheet with positions (x,y), receive broad excitatory drive (Bonnevie et al., 2013 and Figure 1B), and inhibit one another at a characteristic separation on the neural sheet (Figure 1C).
source: Namely, neurons are arranged in a 2D sheet with positions (x,y), receive broad excitatory drive (Bonnevie et al., 2013 and Figure 1B), and inhibit one another at a characteristic separation on the neural sheet (Figure 1C; see Materials and methods for a complete description).
evidence: This describes the model architecture shown in Figure 1B,C and supported by experimental evidence.

claim: The inhibition distance l is constant within each network but increases from one network to the next along the longitudinal axis of the MEC.
source: In our model, this inhibition distance l is constant within each network but increases from one network to the next along the longitudinal axis of the MEC.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model architecture shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The population activity in each network self-organizes into a triangular grid whose lattice points correspond to peaks in neural activity (Figure 2A).
source: With these features alone, the population activity in each network self-organizes into a triangular grid whose lattice points correspond to peaks in neural activity (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The scale of each network's grid, which we call λ(z), is proportional to that network's inhibition distance l(z) ('uncoupled' simulations in Figure 3A).
source: Importantly, the scale of each network's grid, which we call λ(z), is proportional to that network's inhibition distance l(z) ('uncoupled' simulations in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the uncoupled simulation results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Network grid orientations θ show no consistent pattern across scales and among replicate simulations with different random initial firing rates.
source: Also, network grid orientations θ show no consistent pattern across scales and among replicate simulations with different random initial firing rates.
evidence: This is shown in the uncoupled simulations in Figure 3A (right panel).

claim: The inhibitory connections in each network are slightly modulated by the animal's velocity such that the population activity pattern of each network translates proportionally to animal motion at all times.
source: Following the standard attractor model (Burak and Fiete, 2009), the inhibitory connections in each network are slightly modulated by the animal's velocity such that the population activity pattern of each network translates proportionally to animal motion at all times (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes a feature of the model based on the established Burak-Fiete model.

claim: This modulation allows each network to encode the animal's displacement through a process known as path-integration.
source: This modulation allows each network to encode the animal's displacement through a process known as path-integration, and projects the network grid pattern onto spatial rate maps of single neurons.
evidence: This describes the functional consequence of velocity modulation in the model.

claim: Λ(z) for a neuron from network z is proportional to that network's population grid scale λ(z), and thus also proportional to its inhibition distance l(z) (uncoupled simulations in Figure 3B).
source: Moreover, Λ(z) for a neuron from network z is proportional to that network's population grid scale λ(z), and thus also proportional to its inhibition distance l(z) (uncoupled simulations in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the uncoupled simulation results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Spatial orientations of grids show no clustering in the uncoupled model.
source: Like the network orientations θ discussed above, spatial orientations of grids show no clustering (uncoupled simulations in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in the uncoupled simulations in Figure 3B (right panel).

claim: With an inhibition distance l(z) that increases gradually from one network to the next, proportional changes in network and spatial scales λ(z) and Λ(z) lead to a smooth distribution of grid scales.
source: With an inhibition distance l(z) that increases gradually from one network to the next (Figure 1C), proportional changes in network and spatial scales λ(z) and Λ(z) lead to a smooth distribution of grid scales (uncoupled simulations in Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the uncoupled simulation results shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: To reproduce the experimentally observed jumps in grid scale between modules, the inhibition distance would also have to undergo discrete, sharp jumps between certain adjacent networks.
source: To reproduce the experimentally observed jumps in grid scale between modules, the inhibition distance would also have to undergo discrete, sharp jumps between certain adjacent networks.
evidence: This is an inference about what would be required in the uncoupled model to produce modules.

claim: A grid system created by disjoint attractor networks will not self-organize into modules.
source: In summary, a grid system created by disjoint attractor networks will not self-organize into modules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the uncoupled simulation results.

claim: Module self-organization can be achieved with excitatory connections from each neuron to those in the preceding network with approximately corresponding neural sheet positions (Figure 1D).
source: Module self-organization can be achieved with one addition to the established features listed above: we introduce excitatory connections from each neuron to those in the preceding network with approximately corresponding neural sheet positions (Figure 1D; see Materials and methods for a complete description).
evidence: This describes the key addition to the model that enables module formation, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A neuron in network z (more ventral) with position (x,y) will excite neurons in network z – 1 (more dorsal) with positions that are within a distance d of position (x,y).
source: That is, a neuron in network z (more ventral) with position (x,y) will excite neurons in network z – 1 (more dorsal) with positions that are within a distance d of position (x,y).
evidence: This describes the structure of the excitatory coupling in the model.

claim: The self-organization of triangular grids in the neural sheet and the faithful path-integration that projects these grids onto single neuron spatial rate maps persist after introduction of inter-network coupling (Figure 2G).
source: The self-organization of triangular grids in the neural sheet and the faithful path-integration that projects these grids onto single neuron spatial rate maps persist after introduction of inter-network coupling (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the coupled simulation results shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Network and spatial scales λ(z) and Λ(z) still increase from network z = 1 (dorsal) to network z = 12 (ventral) in the coupled model.
source: Network and spatial scales λ(z) and Λ(z) still increase from network z = 1 (dorsal) to network z = 12 (ventral).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A,B for the coupled model.

claim: For the coupled model, scales exhibit plateaus that are interrupted by large jumps, disrupting their proportionality to inhibition distance l(z).
source: Yet, Figure 3A,B shows that for the coupled model, these scales exhibit plateaus that are interrupted by large jumps, disrupting their proportionality to inhibition distance l(z), which is kept identical to that of the uncoupled system (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the coupled simulation results shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Collecting scales across all networks illustrates that they cluster around certain values in the coupled system while they are smoothly distributed in the uncoupled system.
source: Collecting scales across all networks illustrates that they cluster around certain values in the coupled system while they are smoothly distributed in the uncoupled system.
evidence: This is shown in the histograms in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Multiple networks at various depths z can belong to the same module.
source: Note that multiple networks at various depths z can belong to the same module.
evidence: This is evident from the plateaus in scale shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Coupling causes grid cells that cluster around a certain scale to also cluster around a certain orientation (Figure 3A,B), as seen in experiment (Stensola et al., 2012).
source: Moreover, coupling causes grid cells that cluster around a certain scale to also cluster around a certain orientation (Figure 3A,B), as seen in experiment (Stensola et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the coupled simulation results shown in Figure 3A,B and matches experimental observations.

claim: The uncoupled system does not demonstrate co-modularity of orientation with scale.
source: The uncoupled system does not demonstrate co-modularity of orientation with scale, that is two networks with similar grid scales need not have similar orientations unless this is imposed by an external constraint.
evidence: This is shown in the uncoupled simulations in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Excitatory coupling between grid attractor networks dynamically induces discreteness in grid scales that is co-modular with grid orientation, as observed experimentally (Stensola et al., 2012).
source: In summary, excitatory coupling between grid attractor networks dynamically induces discreteness in grid scales that is co-modular with grid orientation, as observed experimentally (Stensola et al., 2012), and as needed for even coverage of space by the grid map (Sanzeni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by the coupled simulations and experimental citations.

claim: For the coupled system depicted in Figure 2, scale ratios and orientation differences between pairs of adjacent modules consistently take values 1.74 ± 0.02 and 29.5 ± 0.4°, respectively (mean ± s.d.; Figure 3C).
source: For the coupled system depicted in Figure 2, scale ratios and orientation differences between pairs of adjacent modules consistently take values 1.74 ± 0.02 and 29.5 ± 0.4°, respectively (mean ± s.d.; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: These values are robust to a variety of parameter perturbations, coupling architectures, and sources of noise.
source: These values are robust to a variety of parameter perturbations, coupling architectures, and sources of noise.
evidence: This is supported by the robustness analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The same scale ratio of ≈1.7 and orientation difference of ≈30° persist when the inhibition distance profile l(z) is made less or more concave (Figure 4A,B).
source: We can make the inhibition distance profile l(z) less or more concave (Figure 4A,B), or we can implement excitatory connections with different properties by reversing their direction (Figure 4C), including connections in both directions (Figure 4D), or allowing the coupling spread to vary with network depth (Figure 4E). In each case, the same scale ratio of ≈1.7 and orientation difference of ≈30° persist.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the robustness analysis shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The same scale ratio of ≈1.7 and orientation difference of ≈30° persist when excitatory connections are reversed in direction (Figure 4C).
source: We can make the inhibition distance profile l(z) less or more concave (Figure 4A,B), or we can implement excitatory connections with different properties by reversing their direction (Figure 4C), including connections in both directions (Figure 4D), or allowing the coupling spread to vary with network depth (Figure 4E). In each case, the same scale ratio of ≈1.7 and orientation difference of ≈30° persist.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the robustness analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The same scale ratio of ≈1.7 and orientation difference of ≈30° persist when connections are included in both directions (Figure 4D).
source: We can make the inhibition distance profile l(z) less or more concave (Figure 4A,B), or we can implement excitatory connections with different properties by reversing their direction (Figure 4C), including connections in both directions (Figure 4D), or allowing the coupling spread to vary with network depth (Figure 4E). In each case, the same scale ratio of ≈1.7 and orientation difference of ≈30° persist.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the robustness analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The same scale ratio of ≈1.7 and orientation difference of ≈30° persist when the coupling spread varies with network depth (Figure 4E).
source: We can make the inhibition distance profile l(z) less or more concave (Figure 4A,B), or we can implement excitatory connections with different properties by reversing their direction (Figure 4C), including connections in both directions (Figure 4D), or allowing the coupling spread to vary with network depth (Figure 4E). In each case, the same scale ratio of ≈1.7 and orientation difference of ≈30° persist.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the robustness analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The number of neurons can be reduced by a factor of 9 without affecting the scale ratio and orientation difference (Figure 4F).
source: We can also reduce the number of neurons by a factor of 9 without affecting the scale ratio and orientation difference (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the robustness analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Similar results are obtained with neural inputs corrupted by independent Gaussian noise (Figure 4G).
source: Similar results are obtained with neural inputs corrupted by independent Gaussian noise (Figure 4G) and with randomly shifted excitatory connections, which adds another form of coupling imprecision in addition to spread (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the robustness analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Similar results are obtained with randomly shifted excitatory connections (Figure 4H).
source: Similar results are obtained with neural inputs corrupted by independent Gaussian noise (Figure 4G) and with randomly shifted excitatory connections, which adds another form of coupling imprecision in addition to spread (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the robustness analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Simulations with spiking dynamics following Burak and Fiete (2009) also demonstrate a preference for scale ratios of ≈1.7 and orientation differences of ≈30°, albeit with greater variability (Figure 4I).
source: Finally, simulations with spiking dynamics following Burak and Fiete (2009) also demonstrate a preference for scale ratios of ≈1.7 and orientation differences of ≈30°, albeit with greater variability (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spiking simulations shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Coupling causes areas of high activity in network z to preferentially excite corresponding areas in network z – 1, which encourages adjacent networks to share the same grid pattern.
source: However, coupling causes areas of high activity in network z to preferentially excite corresponding areas in network z – 1, which encourages adjacent networks to share the same grid pattern (z = 10 & 11 in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by the activity overlays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Coupling adds rigidity to the system and provides an opposing 'force' against the changing inhibition distance that attempts to drive changes in grid scale.
source: Thus, coupling adds rigidity to the system and provides an opposing 'force' against the changing inhibition distance that attempts to drive changes in grid scale.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the model dynamics.

claim: This rigidity produces the plateaus in network and spatial scales λ(z) and Λ(z) that delineate modules across multiple networks.
source: This rigidity produces the plateaus in network and spatial scales λ(z) and Λ(z) that delineate modules across multiple networks.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the plateaus observed in Figure 3A,B.

claim: At interfaces between modules, coupling can no longer fully oppose the changing inhibition distance, and the grid pattern changes.
source: At interfaces between modules, coupling can no longer fully oppose the changing inhibition distance, and the grid pattern changes.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the jumps in scale observed at module boundaries.

claim: The rigidity fixes a geometric relationship between the grid patterns of the two networks spanning the interface.
source: However, the rigidity fixes a geometric relationship between the grid patterns of the two networks spanning the interface.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the commensurate lattice relationships observed at module boundaries.

claim: Module interfaces occur between networks z = 4 and 5 and between z = 9 and 10 in the coupled system of Figure 2 and Figure 3.
source: In the coupled system of Figure 2 and Figure 3, module interfaces occur between networks z = 4 and 5 and between z = 9 and 10.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The network population activity overlays of Figure 3D reveal overlap of many activity peaks at module interfaces.
source: The network population activity overlays of Figure 3D reveal overlap of many activity peaks at these interfaces.
evidence: This is an observation from the activity overlays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The more dorsal network (with smaller z) at each interface contains additional small peaks between the shared peaks.
source: However, the more dorsal network (with smaller z) at each interface contains additional small peaks between the shared peaks.
evidence: This is an observation from the activity overlays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Excitatory coupling can compete against a changing inhibition distance to produce a rigid grid system whose 'fractures' exhibit stereotyped commensurate lattice relationships.
source: In summary, excitatory coupling can compete against a changing inhibition distance to produce a rigid grid system whose 'fractures' exhibit stereotyped commensurate lattice relationships.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanism supported by the simulations.

claim: These robust geometric relationships lead to discrete modules with fixed scale ratios and orientation differences.
source: These robust geometric relationships lead to discrete modules with fixed scale ratios and orientation differences.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by the simulations.

claim: Commensurate lattice relationships naturally lead to field-to-field firing rate variability in single neuron spatial rate maps (z = 8 in Figure 2G, for example).
source: In our model, commensurate lattice relationships naturally lead to field-to-field firing rate variability in single neuron spatial rate maps (z = 8 in Figure 2G, for example), another experimentally observed feature of the grid system (Ismakov et al., 2017; Dunn et al., 2017; Diehl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model shown in Figure 2G and supported by experimental citations.

claim: At interfaces between two commensurate lattices, only a subset of population activity peaks in the grid of smaller scale overlap with, and thus receive excitation from, those in the grid of larger scale.
source: At interfaces between two commensurate lattices, only a subset of population activity peaks in the grid of smaller scale overlap with, and thus receive excitation from, those in the grid of larger scale.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for firing rate variability.

claim: The network with smaller grid scale will contain activity peaks of different magnitudes; this heterogeneity is then projected onto the spatial rate maps of its neurons.
source: The network with smaller grid scale will contain activity peaks of different magnitudes; this heterogeneity is then projected onto the spatial rate maps of its neurons.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for firing rate variability.

claim: As the excitation-inhibition balance is varied by changing umag and l(2)/l(1), a number of discretely different relationships appear, which can be summarized in 'phase diagrams' (Figure 5A,B).
source: We find that as the excitation-inhibition balance is varied by changing umag and l(2)/l(1), a number of discretely different relationships appear, which can be summarized in 'phase diagrams' (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is a summary of the parameter exploration shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: By changing the balance between excitation and inhibition, a two-network model yields geometric lattice relationships with various scale ratios and corresponding orientation differences.
source: Thus, by changing the balance between excitation and inhibition, a two-network model yields geometric lattice relationships with various scale ratios and corresponding orientation differences.
evidence: This is a summary of the parameter exploration shown in Figure 5.

claim: All the commensurate relationships (Figure 5C) and almost the entire range of discommensurate relationships (Figure 5D) have scale ratios that fall in the range of experimental measurements, which is roughly 1.2–2.0 (Stensola et al., 2012; Barry et al., 2007; Krupic et al., 2015).
source: All the commensurate relationships (Figure 5C) and almost the entire range of discommensurate relationships (Figure 5D) have scale ratios that fall in the range of experimental measurements, which is roughly 1.2–2.0 (Stensola et al., 2012; Barry et al., 2007; Krupic et al., 2015).
evidence: This compares the model predictions to experimental measurements.

claim: The scale ratios and orientation differences in both the commensurate and discommensurate cases are robust against activity noise and coupling noise (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
source: The scale ratios and orientation differences in both the commensurate and discommensurate cases are robust against activity noise and coupling noise (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the robustness analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Discommensurate lattices have a range of allowed geometries (Figure 5D,E), but they can still produce modules in a full 12-network grid system with a preferred scale ratio and orientation difference.
source: As mentioned above, discommensurate lattices have a range of allowed geometries (Figure 5D,E), but they can still produce modules in a full 12-network grid system with a preferred scale ratio and orientation difference.
evidence: This is a summary of the discommensurate lattice analysis.

claim: Discommensurate lattice values do not cluster as strongly as they do for a commensurate relationship, which is geometrically precise.
source: However, these values do not cluster as strongly as they do for a commensurate relationship, which is geometrically precise.
evidence: This is an observation about the difference between commensurate and discommensurate lattices.

claim: Network activity overlays of discommensurate simulations reveal grids obeying discommensurate relationships (Figure 6B,C).
source: Network activity overlays of these new simulations reveal grids obeying discommensurate relationships (Figure 6B,C), which are projected onto single neuron spatial rate maps through faithful path-integration (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: The discommensurate system demonstrates greater variation in scale and orientation (Figure 6D) than the commensurate system of Figure 3 does.
source: Across replicate simulations with identical parameter values but different random initial firing rates, the discommensurate system demonstrates greater variation in scale and orientation (Figure 6D) than the commensurate system of Figure 3 does.
evidence: This is a comparison between the discommensurate and commensurate simulation results.

claim: Analysis of each replicate simulation reveals clustering with well-defined modules (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
source: Nevertheless, analysis of each replicate simulation reveals clustering with well-defined modules (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: These modules have scale ratio 1.39 ± 0.10 and orientation difference 6.7 ± 3.5° (mean ± s.d.; Figure 6F).
source: These modules have scale ratio 1.39 ± 0.10 and orientation difference 6.7 ± 3.5° (mean ± s.d.; Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the discommensurate simulation results shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The preferred scale ratio agrees well with the mean value observed experimentally in Stensola et al. (2012).
source: The preferred scale ratio agrees well with the mean value observed experimentally in Stensola et al. (2012).
evidence: This compares the discommensurate model prediction to experimental measurements.

claim: Excitatory coupling, especially when the spread is larger, provides enough rigidity in the discommensurate system to cluster scale ratios and orientation differences but not enough to prevent variations in these values.
source: Conceptually, we can interpret the greater spread of scales and orientations in terms of coupling rigidity. Excitatory coupling, especially when the spread is larger, provides enough rigidity in the discommensurate system to cluster scale ratios and orientation differences but not enough to prevent variations in these values.
